title: Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT)
summary: Rapid 30-second across-the-room assessment using the PAT to identify the sick child.
equipment: Eyes and ears (no equipment needed for initial PAT)
steps: Observe from a distance (do not touch yet — avoids fear response that alters assessment).
A — Appearance (TICLS): Tone (limp vs. normal), Interactibility (responsive vs. unresponsive), Consolability, Look/Gaze (tracks caregiver), Speech/Cry (strong vs. weak/absent).
B — Breathing: Look for abnormal positioning (tripod, sniffing), visible retractions (subcostal, intercostal, suprasternal), paradoxical breathing, nasal flaring, head bobbing (infant).
C — Circulation to skin: Look for pallor, mottling, cyanosis.
Interpret findings:
Abnormal A only → Primary CNS or metabolic problem.
Abnormal B only → Primary respiratory problem.
Abnormal C only → Primary cardiovascular/shock problem.
Abnormal A + B → Respiratory failure.
Abnormal A + C → Shock causing end-organ dysfunction.
Abnormal A + B + C → Cardiopulmonary failure — most critical.
Proceed immediately with hands-on assessment based on PAT findings.
Apply pediatric-specific norms for HR, RR, and BP based on age group.
safetyTips: A quiet, alert, and comforted child is rarely critically ill.
A limp, unresponsive, or inconsolable child requires immediate intervention.
Never assume a quiet child is comfortable — they may be too ill to cry.
documentation: PAT findings (appearance, work of breathing, circulation)
Vital signs with age-appropriate norms noted
keyTakeaways: Abnormal appearance = brain not getting what it needs

title: Pediatric Weight-Based Medication Dosing Verification
summary: Safely calculating and verifying weight-based pediatric medication doses before administration.
equipment: Dosing reference (Harriet Lane Handbook or facility drug guide)
steps: Obtain accurate weight in KILOGRAMS. Document the date and measurement method.
Verify order includes weight-based dose (mg/kg or mcg/kg/min).
Calculate: Dose = weight (kg) × dose per kg. Example: 10mg/kg × 20kg = 200mg.
Verify calculated dose against reference range maximum (e.g., max single dose, max daily dose).
Check concentration available: if drug is 250mg/5mL, calculate volume to draw up.
Perform independent double-check with second nurse for high-alert medications (antibiotics, opioids, chemotherapy, electrolytes).
Round appropriately — do not assume decimal points are correct. 10-fold dosing errors are the most common fatal pediatric error.
Verify the FIVE rights and route before administration.
For continuous infusions: verify drug, concentration, dose rate, and pump settings independently.
Document dose in mg/kg administered, not just total mg.
safetyTips: Decimal point errors kill children — always write 0.5mg, never .5mg. Never write 5.0mg.
When in doubt about a dose, call pharmacy or the provider — never guess.
Use pre-printed or electronic dosing tools when available to reduce calculation errors.
keyTakeaways: Decimal point errors are the #1 pediatric medication error
Independent double-check for all high-alert meds

title: Pediatric Fever Assessment & Management
summary: Assessing and managing fever in pediatric patients, including age-specific thresholds and antipyretic administration.
equipment: Age-appropriate thermometer (rectal for <3 months, temporal/axillary for older)
steps: Assess temperature using appropriate method:
<3 months: rectal temperature is gold standard.
3 months–4 years: temporal artery or tympanic.
>4 years: oral or tympanic.
Fever thresholds: ≥38.0°C (100.4°F) rectal; ≥37.5°C axillary/temporal.
RED FLAGS requiring immediate provider notification:
Any fever in infant <28 days (neonatal sepsis risk).
Fever + petechiae/purpura (meningococcemia).
Fever + bulging fontanel (meningitis).
Febrile seizure.
Fever in immunocompromised child (oncology, transplant).
Non-pharmacologic: lightweight clothing, room-temperature fluids, tepid sponging (NOT ice water).
Pharmacologic: acetaminophen 10–15mg/kg q4–6h OR ibuprofen 5–10mg/kg q6–8h (>6 months only). Verify weight-based dose.
Reassess temperature 30–60 minutes after antipyretic.
Ensure hydration — encourage age-appropriate fluids.
safetyTips: NEVER give aspirin to children (Reye's syndrome risk).
Do not alternate antipyretics without provider order — risk of dosing errors.
Fever itself is not dangerous below 41°C — it is a sign, not the disease.
documentation: Time of antipyretic given, dose, and route
keyTakeaways: Any fever in newborn <28 days is an emergency

title: Newborn Umbilical Cord Care
summary: Providing proper care to the umbilical cord stump to prevent infection and promote separation.
equipment: Clean water (dry cord care is current evidence-based standard)
steps: Assess the umbilical cord stump at each diaper change: color, odor, signs of infection.
Normal cord: yellow-green at birth, dries and turns black/brown over 1–3 weeks.
Dry cord care (WHO and AAP recommendation): keep the stump dry. No alcohol or antiseptics unless in high-risk settings.
Keep stump exposed to air — fold diaper below the cord level.
Sponge baths only until cord falls off (avoid submersion baths).
INFECTION signs — notify provider: redness or warmth of surrounding skin (periumbilical erythema), foul smell, purulent discharge, fever.
Normal cord separation: 7–21 days. Small amount of dried blood at separation is normal.
Do NOT pull or cut the cord — let it separate naturally.
Granuloma (small pink nodule after cord falls off): refer to provider — may require silver nitrate treatment.
safetyTips: Omphalitis (cord infection) can rapidly lead to neonatal sepsis — treat red, warm, swollen periumbilical skin as urgent.
Never submerge infant in water until cord has completely separated.
Alcohol-based cleaning is no longer recommended — it delays separation.
keyTakeaways: Redness of surrounding skin = omphalitis — notify provider

title: Pediatric Resuscitation (PALS Framework)
summary: Recognizing and initiating resuscitation in pediatric patients using the PALS systematic approach.
steps: Assess safety. Tap and shout — is child responsive?
If unresponsive: call for help / activate code. Get AED/defibrillator.
Open airway (head-tilt chin-lift; jaw thrust if trauma). Look, listen, feel for breathing.
If not breathing: give 2 rescue breaths with appropriate-size BVM — watch for chest rise.
Check pulse: carotid (>1 year), brachial or femoral (infant) for up to 10 seconds.
Start CPR if no pulse or HR <60 with poor perfusion:
Compression rate: 100–120/min. Depth: 1/3 AP diameter of chest.
Ratio: 30:2 (single rescuer) or 15:2 (two rescuers for children).
Use Broselow tape to estimate weight-based drug doses and equipment sizes.
Establish IV or IO access — IO is preferred if IV unsuccessful after 60–90 seconds.
Administer epinephrine 0.01mg/kg IV/IO (max 1mg) every 3–5 minutes for cardiac arrest.
Defibrillate VF/pVT: 2 J/kg first shock, 4 J/kg subsequent. Use pediatric pads if <10kg.
Identify and treat reversible causes (H's and T's).
safetyTips: Respiratory failure is the most common cause of pediatric arrest — airway is priority.
IO access is lifesaving — do not delay drug delivery for IV attempts.
Broselow tape reduces dosing errors significantly — always use it.
keyTakeaways: IO when IV fails — do not delay
